display_name: Epsilon-greedy policy over a tabular Q (legal-action aware)
short_description: Chooses a greedy action of the agent's own action-value table with probability 1 - epsilon (ties split evenly) and a uniformly random legal action with probability epsilon.

textbook.reference: Sutton, R. S. & Barto, A. G. (2018). Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.). MIT Press, sec. 2.2-2.3 (epsilon-greedy) and sec. 5.4 (epsilon-soft policies)

pedagogy.motivation: An agent that always takes the action it currently believes is best never discovers that another action might be better: its estimates of the untried actions are never corrected. Epsilon-greedy is the simplest fix. Most of the time the agent exploits what it knows, but with a small probability epsilon it explores by picking a legal action at random, so every legal action keeps being tried.
assumptions: Actions are discrete and the observation maps to one row of the value table (DiscreteStateCodec).
The set of legal actions L comes from the current view's ActionMask; illegal actions get probability exactly 0.
Ties among the best legal actions are broken by splitting the greedy mass evenly, not by picking the first column.
Randomness comes only from the RandStream handed in by the agent's host: exactly one uniform draw per decision.
pedagogy.data_model: The policy reads Q(s, a) for the current state s over the legal set L. The greedy set is G = argmax over a in L of Q(s, a). Every legal action receives epsilon / |L|; each greedy action additionally receives (1 - epsilon) / |G|. The distribution is reported with the decision (Probabilities) together with the probability of the action actually taken (Likelihood), which off-policy estimators need.
pedagogy.what_is_missing: The true action values are unknown; Q is only the current estimate, updated by the agent's learner. Epsilon trades using the estimate (exploitation) against gathering the data that would improve it (exploration).
pedagogy.how_it_solves: 1. Encode the observation to a row of Q. 2. Take the legal set L from the view's mask. 3. Find the greedy set G among the legal actions (keeping ties). 4. Build p(a) = epsilon/|L| + (1 - epsilon)/|G| for a in G, epsilon/|L| for the other legal actions, 0 for illegal ones. 5. Draw one uniform u from the host's stream and return the first action whose cumulative probability exceeds u (inverse CDF).

policy.label: Epsilon-greedy over the legal set
policy.description: Probability of action a in state s for a legal action; illegal actions have probability 0.

greedy_set.label: Greedy set
greedy_set.description: All legal actions whose value equals the best legal value; ties are kept and share the greedy mass.

inverse_cdf.label: Inverse-CDF sampling
inverse_cdf.description: One uniform draw selects the action; columns with zero probability can never be selected.

Symbols.Description: probability that the policy chooses action a in state s
set of actions legal in the current view (from its ActionMask)
greedy set: legal actions with the largest Q(s, a)
the agent's current action-value estimate (shared with its learner)
indicator: 1 if a is greedy, 0 otherwise
the single uniform random number drawn from the host's stream per decision

parameters.name: Epsilon
parameters.description: Probability of choosing uniformly among the legal actions instead of greedily.
parameters.effect: Larger epsilon explores more (slower to exploit, but less likely to lock onto a wrong greedy action); epsilon = 0 is purely greedy, epsilon = 1 is uniformly random over the legal set.

parameters.name: StateCodec
parameters.description: Maps a discrete observation to a row of Q; out-of-range observations are an error.
parameters.effect: Must match the environment's observation space (N and Start).

complexity.training: O(1) (the policy does not train; the learner updates Q)
complexity.memory: O(1) beyond the shared S x A table

strengths: Simple, with a single interpretable parameter.
Every legal action keeps a non-zero probability, which Q-learning's convergence argument needs.
Reports exact action probabilities, so importance-sampling corrections are possible.
weaknesses: Explores uniformly: a known-terrible action is tried as often as a promising one.
A fixed epsilon never stops exploring, so the behaviour is never exactly greedy.
Only for discrete actions and tabular states.
when_to_use: Use as the default behaviour policy for tabular control (Q-learning, Sarsa) when the action set is small and discrete. Prefer softmax or optimistic initialisation when uniform exploration is wasteful, and decay epsilon if a near-greedy final policy is needed.
references: Sutton, R. S. & Barto, A. G. (2018). Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.), sec. 2.2, 5.4, 6.5.
Watkins, C. J. C. H. (1989). Learning from Delayed Rewards. PhD thesis, University of Cambridge.
